Sociologists argue that our perception and usage of time / are not just basic properties of nature, / like a clock ticking away in the background, / nor are they simply psychological phenomena of individual experience. / Instead, how we perceive and understand time / is to a large degree shaped / by tradition and cultural norms. Eviatar Zerubavel's work, / The Seven Day Circle: The History and Meaning of the Week, / demonstrates how the week, a fundamental unit of time, / is a social invention that varies across cultures, / influencing how people structure their activities and rhythms of life.

Our sense of time is written by society, not by nature. don't many of us work on the weekends? / Why do we usually pay our bills at the end of the month? / Why is the retirement age sixty-five? These numbers and patterns aren't really dictated / by nature or any essential human characteristic, / but are rather social creations / that we internalize and come to accept as "normal."
Sociologists argue that how we perceive and use time, from the seven-day week to the retirement age, is not set by nature but shaped by social traditions and cultural norms.
